\title{The Block-Count Cap: Universal Ceilings for Rank Correlation Under Ties,\\
with Application to the 2-adic Zero-Fit Dial}
\author{Aristotle}
\date{September 1, 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
A statistic that takes only finitely many values imposes a hard, purely combinatorial ceiling
on the rank correlation it can achieve with any response. We analyse that ceiling as a
functional of the \emph{tie profile} $L=(m_1,\dots,m_K)$, the multiset of tie-class sizes on a
sample of size $n=\sum_j m_j$. Three results form the core. A \emph{continuum sandwich}: for
$n\ge2$,
$1 - C(L)/n^3 \le \rmax(L) \le 1 - C(L)/n^3 + 1/n^2$ where $C(L)=\sum_j m_j^3$, so the exact
discrete ceiling and its continuum idealisation differ by at most $1/n^2$, uniformly over all
profiles. A \emph{power-mean bound} $n^3 \le K^2 C(L)$, with equality exactly at the flat
profile, proved by induction from the cubic factorisation
$(1+s)^2(s^2u^3+v^3)-s^2(u+v)^3=(v-su)^2[(1+2s)v+s(2+s)u]$. Combining them, the
\emph{block-count cap} $\rmax(L)\le 1-1/K^2+1/n^2$, which depends on the number of tie classes
alone and is sharp to within $1/n^2$. We apply this to the 2-adic zero-fit dial
$T(x)=\nu_2(x)$ on uniform $b$-bit draws, whose profile is $(2^{b-1},\dots,2,1,1)$ with cubic
moment $(8^b+6)/7$ and unweighted ceiling $\sqrt{6/7}$. For two-level weightings the sharp
ceiling is $\kappa^\star = 1-1/(1+\sqrt7)^2=0.9247639\ldots$, attained only at the irrational
ratio $q=\sqrt7\,p$; for arbitrary weightings the block-count cap applies verbatim, since a
weighting never creates tie classes, giving $\rmax \le 1-1/3249+2^{-112}$ at bit-length $56$.
Applied to a recorded fresh-seed replication (pooled $\rho=0.669$, CI $[0.650,0.690]$, weighted
advantage $+0.045$ against a $+0.05$ bar), the theory shows the entire reweighting budget on
the $\rho$ scale is $(0.0358,0.0359)$ --- over seven times the $0.005$ shortfall --- so the
negative verdict reflects the response variable, not the dial's tie geometry.
\end{abstract}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} rank correlation, tie correction, power-mean inequality, 2-adic
valuation, trailing-zero statistic, tie profile, extremal combinatorics, sharp bounds.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Coarse statistics and their ceilings}

Many practical probes of a complex system are \emph{coarse by design}: they map a rich state
into a small number of readings, trading resolution for interpretability and cost. A popcount,
a bucketised timing, a discretised difficulty score, a valuation of an integer --- all take
finitely many values, typically with very unequal frequencies.

Coarseness has a price. When a statistic takes the same value on many observations those
observations are \emph{tied}: no rank-based procedure can order them. Standard rank-correlation
coefficients handle this with midranks, and the resulting coefficient carries a \emph{tie
correction}. That correction is an upper bound on measurable association: even against a
perfectly monotone response, a heavily tied statistic cannot report a correlation near $1$.

We study that bound as a mathematical object and ask three questions. How much does the exact
discrete ceiling differ from its continuum surrogate? Over all profiles with a fixed number of
classes, what is the best possible ceiling? Can \emph{reweighting} the sample evade the bound?
The answers are: at most $1/n^2$; exactly $1-1/K^2$ up to $1/n^2$, attained at the flat
profile; and no.

\subsection{The motivating experiment}

The motivating instrument is the \emph{zero-fit dial}: for an integer $x$, the statistic
$T(x)=\nu_2(x)$, the number of trailing zero bits. On uniform draws from $\{0,\dots,2^b-1\}$
the tie profile is the geometric cascade
$L_b=(2^{b-1},2^{b-2},\dots,2,1,1)$, with $K=b+1$ classes and mass $n=2^b$.

A fresh-seed replication of a bit-length-$56$ cell across three seeds recorded pooled
$\rho(T,\text{rate})=0.669$ with CI $[0.650,0.690]$, inside the pre-registered validation band
$[0.55,0.85]$: the primary hypothesis replicated on all three seeds. The secondary hypothesis
--- that the trailing-zero statistic beats a plain popcount baseline by more than $+0.05$ ---
failed: the pooled advantage was $+0.045$ and only one of three seeds cleared the bar, so the
weighted edge was declared not established. Such a verdict admits two explanations: the dial
genuinely lacks the edge, or its tie geometry capped the advantage by construction.
Distinguishing them requires the dial's exact ceiling, including under reweighting.

\section{Setup and definitions}

\begin{definition}[Tie profile]
A \emph{tie profile} is a finite list $L=(m_1,\dots,m_K)$ of nonnegative integers. Its
\emph{length} $K=|L|$ is the number of tie classes, its \emph{mass} is $n=n(L)=\sum_j m_j$,
and its \emph{cubic moment} is $C(L)=\sum_{j=1}^K m_j^3$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Tie correction and ceiling]
The Kendall tie correction of $L$ is
$\tie(L)=\tfrac1{12}\sum_j (m_j^3-m_j)=\tfrac{C(L)-n}{12}$, and for $n\ge2$ the \emph{ceiling}
of $L$ --- the maximum squared Spearman rank correlation achievable between a statistic with
profile $L$ and any response, attained when the response is monotone in the statistic --- is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:law}
\rmax(L) \;=\; 1-\frac{12\,\tie(L)}{n^3-n} \;=\; 1-\frac{C(L)-n}{n^3-n}.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

Equation~\eqref{eq:law} is the \emph{tie-attenuation law}; it depends on $L$ only through
$(C(L),n)$. If all $m_j=1$ then $C(L)=n$ and $\rmax=1$; if $K=1$ then $C(L)=n^3$ and
$\rmax=0$.

\begin{definition}[Flat profile]
For $K,m\ge1$, the \emph{flat profile} $F_{K,m}$ is the constant list of $K$ blocks of size
$m$; its mass is $Km$ and $C(F_{K,m})=Km^3$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Dyadic profile]
Set $D_0=(1)$ and $D_{b+1}=(2^b)\frown D_b$, so $D_b=(2^{b-1},\dots,2,1,1)$ for $b\ge1$. This
is the profile of the zero-fit dial on uniform $b$-bit draws.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Weighting]
A \emph{weight vector} is a list $W=(w_1,\dots,w_M)$ of nonnegative integers, acting
coordinatewise on a profile $L$ with $|L|\le M$ by
$W\odot L=(w_1m_1,\dots,w_Km_K)$. Operationally, giving every observation in class $j$
multiplicity $w_j$ produces a sample with profile $W\odot L$.
\end{definition}

The crucial structural facts are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weight}
n(W\odot L)=\sum_j w_jm_j,\qquad C(W\odot L)=\sum_j w_j^3m_j^3,\qquad |W\odot L|=|L|.
\end{equation}
Mass scales linearly in the weights, the cubic moment cubically --- so reweighting is a genuine
lever on the ceiling --- and the number of classes does not change at all, which is why the
main theorem applies to every weighting scheme at once.

\begin{lemma}[Elementary moment bounds]\label{lem:moment}
For every profile $L$, $\;n(L)\le C(L)\le n(L)^3$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For the left inequality, $m\le m^3$ for every nonnegative integer $m$; sum. For the right,
induct on length: with $m$ the head and $S$ the tail mass,
$(m+S)^3=m^3+S^3+3mS(m+S)\ge m^3+S^3\ge m^3+C(\text{tail})$.
\end{proof}

\section{The continuum sandwich}

Formula~\eqref{eq:law} is exact but awkward: the $-m_j$ and $-n$ terms are discrete corrections
obstructing clean optimisation. The natural surrogate is the \emph{continuum ceiling}
$\widetilde\rho^{\,2}(L)=1-C(L)/n^3$, which depends only on the relative frequencies $m_j/n$.
The discrete ceiling always \emph{exceeds} the continuum one, so a cap proved for
$\widetilde\rho^{\,2}$ is not automatically a cap for $\rmax$: a limit statement is not a
finite-length statement. The next theorem closes that gap.

\begin{theorem}[Continuum sandwich]\label{thm:sandwich}
For every tie profile $L$ with mass $n\ge2$,
\[
1-\frac{C(L)}{n^3} \;\le\; \rmax(L) \;\le\; 1-\frac{C(L)}{n^3}+\frac{1}{n^2}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $C=C(L)$, $A=\frac{C-n}{n^3-n}$, $B=\frac{C}{n^3}$, so $\rmax=1-A$ and the surrogate is
$1-B$. Both denominators are positive since $n\ge2$.

\emph{Lower half} ($A\le B$): cross-multiplying, $A\le B$ is equivalent to
$n^3(C-n)\le C(n^3-n)$, i.e.\ $-n^4\le -nC$, i.e.\ $C\le n^3$, which is
Lemma~\ref{lem:moment}.

\emph{Upper half} ($B-1/n^2\le A$): the identity
$\frac{C}{n^3}-\frac{1}{n^2}=\frac{C-n}{n^3}$ holds exactly, and $C\ge n$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:moment}, so the numerator is nonnegative; since $0<n^3-n<n^3$, shrinking the
denominator increases the fraction, giving
$\frac{C-n}{n^3}\le\frac{C-n}{n^3-n}=A$.
\end{proof}

The sandwich width $1/n^2$ is uniform over all profiles and independent of $K$ and the block
sizes. For the dial, $n=2^b$ gives width $4^{-b}$; at $b=56$ this is
$2^{-112}\approx1.93\times10^{-34}$. Any continuum-level cap is therefore a finite-length cap
at negligible cost.

\section{The power-mean bound and the block-count cap}

\subsection{A cubic factorisation}

\begin{lemma}[Cubic weight identity]\label{lem:cubic}
For all real $s,u,v$,
\[
(1+s)^2\left(s^2u^3+v^3\right)-s^2(u+v)^3
= (v-su)^2\Big[(1+2s)v+s(2+s)u\Big].
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand both sides; they agree coefficientwise.
\end{proof}

For $s,u,v\ge0$ the right-hand side is a perfect square times a nonnegative linear form, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cubicineq}
s^2(u+v)^3 \;\le\; (1+s)^2\left(s^2u^3+v^3\right),
\end{equation}
with equality precisely when $v=su$ (for $s>0$, $(u,v)\ne(0,0)$). This identity does double
duty: with $s$ a real weight ratio it yields the sharp $\sqrt7$ constant of
Section~\ref{sec:dial}; with $s=K$ an integer block count it yields the power-mean bound.

\subsection{The power-mean bound}

\begin{theorem}[Power-mean bound]\label{thm:powermean}
For every tie profile $L$ with $K=|L|$ blocks and mass $n=n(L)$,
\[
n^3 \;\le\; K^2\,C(L),
\]
with equality if and only if $L$ is flat.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
This is the power-mean inequality $\left(\tfrac1K\sum m_j\right)^3\le\tfrac1K\sum m_j^3$; we
give the inductive proof, which exposes the same factorisation as Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic}.

Induct on the length. The empty list is trivial. For $L=(m)\frown L'$ with $K'=|L'|$,
$S=n(L')$, $C'=C(L')$, the hypothesis is $S^3\le K'^2C'$ and the goal is
$(m+S)^3\le(K'+1)^2(m^3+C')$. If $K'=0$ then $S=0$ and the goal is $m^3\le m^3$. If $K'\ge1$,
apply \eqref{eq:cubicineq} with $s=K'$, $u=m$, $v=S$:
\[
K'^2(m+S)^3 \;\le\; (1+K')^2\left(K'^2m^3+S^3\right)
\;\le\; (1+K')^2\left(K'^2m^3+K'^2C'\right),
\]
and divide by $K'^2>0$.

Equality: the slack in \eqref{eq:cubicineq} is $(S-K'm)^2$ times a positive form, so equality
forces $S=K'm$, i.e.\ the head equals the mean of the tail; propagating down the induction
forces all blocks equal. Conversely $F_{K,m}$ gives $n^3=K^3m^3=K^2\cdot Km^3=K^2C$.
\end{proof}

Equivalently, for $K,n\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:frac}
\frac{1}{K^2}\;\le\;\frac{C(L)}{n^3}.
\end{equation}

\subsection{The main theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Block-count cap]\label{thm:cap}
For every tie profile $L$ with $K$ blocks and mass $n\ge2$,
\[
\rmax(L) \;\le\; 1-\frac{1}{K^2}+\frac{1}{n^2}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine the upper half of Theorem~\ref{thm:sandwich} with \eqref{eq:frac}:
$\rmax\le 1-C/n^3+1/n^2\le 1-1/K^2+1/n^2$. Positivity of $K$ and $n$ follows from $n\ge2$.
\end{proof}

The bound mentions the block sizes nowhere: whatever the shape of the profile, the ceiling is
governed by the class count alone, up to $1/n^2$.

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]\label{thm:sharp}
For $K\ge2$, $m\ge1$, the flat profile $F_{K,m}$ (mass $n=Km\ge2$) satisfies
\[
1-\frac{1}{K^2}\;\le\;\rmax(F_{K,m})\;\le\;1-\frac{1}{K^2}+\frac{1}{n^2}.
\]
Hence the constant $1-1/K^2$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:cap} cannot be lowered.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The upper bound is Theorem~\ref{thm:cap} with $|F_{K,m}|=K$. For the lower bound use the lower
half of Theorem~\ref{thm:sandwich} with the exact evaluation
$C(F_{K,m})/n^3=Km^3/(Km)^3=1/K^2$.
\end{proof}

Thus $\sup\{\rmax(L):|L|=K,\ n(L)=n\}=1-1/K^2+O(n^{-2})$, attained (up to that correction) at
the flat profile. As $K$ grows the cap tends to $1$: adding classes, and only adding classes,
buys resolution.

\section{The 2-adic dial and the $\sqrt7$ optimum}\label{sec:dial}

\subsection{The unweighted ceiling}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:dyadic}
The dyadic profile $D_b$ has $|D_b|=b+1$, mass $n=2^b$, and cubic moment
$C(D_b)=\dfrac{8^b+6}{7}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Length and mass are immediate inductions from $D_{b+1}=(2^b)\frown D_b$. For the moment,
$C(D_{b+1})=8^b+C(D_b)$ and $8^{b+1}+6=7\cdot8^b+(8^b+6)$; the base case $C(D_0)=1=(1+6)/7$
checks.
\end{proof}

Hence the continuum ceiling of the dial is $1-\frac{8^b+6}{7\cdot8^b}\to 6/7$, and by
Theorem~\ref{thm:sandwich},
\[
\rho_{\max}(D_b)=\sqrt{6/7}+O(4^{-b})=0.9258201\ldots+O(4^{-b}).
\]
The dominant odd class, holding half the mass, permanently costs the dial one seventh of its
squared resolving power, uniformly in $b$.

\subsection{Stratified weightings}

\begin{definition}
For $p,q\ge1$ the \emph{stratified weighting} of the bit-length-$b$ dial weights the dominant
class (mass $2^b$) by $p$ and every deeper class by $q$:
$W_b(p,q)=(p\,2^b)\frown q\!\cdot\!D_b$. Note $W_b(1,1)=D_{b+1}$: uniform weighting merely
advances the bit-length.
\end{definition}

By \eqref{eq:weight}, $n(W_b(p,q))=(p+q)2^b$ and
$C(W_b(p,q))=p^38^b+q^3\frac{8^b+6}{7}$, so the exact ceiling is a closed form in $p,q,2^b$.

\begin{theorem}[Stratified ceiling]\label{thm:strat}
For fixed $p,q\ge1$,
\[
\lim_{b\to\infty}\rmax\big(W_b(p,q)\big)=\kappa(p,q):=1-\frac{p^3+q^3/7}{(p+q)^3}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Substitute the closed forms into \eqref{eq:law}, divide numerator and denominator by $8^b$ and
let $b\to\infty$; the $+6/7$ and the discrete $-n$ terms are $O(8^{-b})$ and $O(2^{-2b})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Weighting strictly helps]
For every $b\ge2$, $\rmax\big(W_b(1,3)\big)>\rmax\big(W_b(1,1)\big)=\rmax\big(D_{b+1}\big)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Both sides are explicit rational functions of $2^b$; their difference is a ratio of polynomials
whose numerator is positive for $2^b\ge4$. Conceptually, tripling the deep classes dilutes the
dominant block, strictly decreasing $C/n^3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$\sqrt7$ cap, with equality case]\label{thm:sqrt7}
For all $p>0$, $q\ge0$,
\[
\kappa(p,q)\;\le\;\kappa^\star:=1-\frac{1}{\left(1+\sqrt7\right)^2},
\]
with equality if and only if $q=\sqrt7\,p$. Numerically $\kappa^\star=0.9247639\ldots$ and
$\sqrt{\kappa^\star}=0.9616465\ldots$
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $\kappa(p,q)=1-\frac{7p^3+q^3}{7(p+q)^3}$; maximising $\kappa$ is minimising the
fraction. Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic} with $s=\sqrt7$, $u=p$, $v=q$ gives
\[
(1+\sqrt7)^2\left(7p^3+q^3\right)-7(p+q)^3
=\left(q-\sqrt7p\right)^2\Big[(1+2\sqrt7)q+\sqrt7(2+\sqrt7)p\Big]\;\ge\;0,
\]
the bracket being positive for $p>0$, $q\ge0$. Rearranging gives
$\frac{7p^3+q^3}{7(p+q)^3}\ge\frac{1}{(1+\sqrt7)^2}$, and the slack vanishes iff $q=\sqrt7p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No rational weighting is optimal]
Since $\sqrt7\notin\mathbb{Q}$, every rational weight ratio $q/p$ satisfies
$\kappa(p,q)<\kappa^\star$ strictly. The continued-fraction convergent $q/p=37/14$ realises
$\kappa^\star$ to within $10^{-7}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-length sharpness]
At every finite bit-length $b$ and for all $p,q\ge1$,
\[
\rmax\big(W_b(p,q)\big)\;\le\;\kappa(p,q)+\frac{1}{4\cdot4^b}\;\le\;\kappa^\star+4^{-(b+1)}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:sandwich} bounds the discrete ceiling by the continuum one plus
$1/n^2=1/((p+q)^24^b)\le1/(4\cdot4^b)$; Theorem~\ref{thm:sqrt7} caps the continuum value.
\end{proof}

At $b=56$: no stratified weighting whatsoever reaches $\kappa^\star+10^{-33}$, i.e.\ no
stratified weighted binary dial can report $\rho>0.9616465$.

\subsection{The radix law}

The constant $7$ is not special to binary; it is the cubic sum of a geometric cascade of ratio
$1/g$. For a radix $g>1$ define the $g$-adic profile $D_b^{(g)}$ with block sizes
$(g-1)g^{b-1},\dots,(g-1),1$ and set
\[
\kappa_g=\frac{g^3-1}{(g-1)^3},\qquad \kappa_2=7,\quad \kappa_{10}=\tfrac{111}{81}.
\]
The limiting cubic-moment fraction is $1/\kappa_g$, the stratified ceiling is
$\kappa^{(g)}(p,q)=1-\frac{p^3+q^3/\kappa_g}{(p+q)^3}$, and its sharp maximum is
$1-1/(1+\sqrt{\kappa_g})^2$, attained at $q=\sqrt{\kappa_g}\,p$.

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity of the weighting gain]
Let $G(\kappa)=\dfrac1\kappa-\dfrac1{(1+\sqrt\kappa)^2}$ be the improvement in squared ceiling
bought by optimal stratified weighting. Then $G(\kappa)>0$ for all $\kappa>0$ and $G$ is
strictly decreasing.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With $\kappa=s^2$, $s>0$,
$G(s^2)=\frac1{s^2}-\frac1{(1+s)^2}=\frac{(1+s)^2-s^2}{s^2(1+s)^2}=\frac{1+2s}{s^2(1+s)^2}>0$,
and the numerator grows linearly while the denominator grows quartically, so $G$ is strictly
decreasing in $s$, hence in $\kappa$.
\end{proof}

For binary, $G(7)=1/7-1/(1+\sqrt7)^2=0.06762$ in squared units, which is the $0.0358$ figure on
the $\rho$ scale.

\section{Arbitrary weightings: the class count is the whole story}

Theorem~\ref{thm:sqrt7} is sharp but conditional: it assumes a two-level weighting. An
adversarial designer would tune all $b+1$ weights independently. The block-count cap removes
the restriction with no loss.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:len}
$|D_b|=b+1$; and for any weight vector $W$ with $|W|\ge b+1$, $|W\odot D_b|=b+1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Universal weighted cap for the dial]\label{thm:univ}
Let $b\ge0$ and let $W$ be any weight vector with $|W|\ge b+1$ such that the reweighted sample
has mass $n\ge2$. Then
\[
\rmax\big(W\odot D_b\big)\;\le\;1-\frac{1}{(b+1)^2}+\frac{1}{n^2}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:len} the reweighted profile has exactly $b+1$ blocks; apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:cap}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Bit-length 56]
For any weight vector $W$ with $|W|\ge57$ and reweighted mass $n\ge2$,
$\rmax(W\odot D_{56})\le 1-\frac{1}{3249}+\frac1{n^2}$; with $n=2^{56}$ this is
$1-1/3249+2^{-112}$, i.e.\ $\rho\le0.9998461\ldots$
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Non-vacuity]
The hypotheses are satisfiable: the all-ones vector of length $57$ has $|W|=57$ and
$W\odot D_{56}=D_{56}$, of mass $2^{56}\ge2$. The cap is a statement with content, not a
vacuous implication.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Optimality of the equalising weighting]
For $b\ge1$ let $E_b$ give the class of numbers with exactly $k$ trailing zeros the weight
$2^k$, so $E_b\odot D_b$ is the flat profile of $b+1$ blocks of size $2^{b-1}$. Then for every
weight vector $W$ with $|W|\ge b+1$ and reweighted mass $n\ge2$,
\[
\rmax\big(W\odot D_b\big)\;\le\;\rmax\big(E_b\odot D_b\big)+\frac{1}{n^2}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The equalising weighting flattens the cascade, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp} its ceiling is at
least $1-1/(b+1)^2$, while Theorem~\ref{thm:univ} caps every competitor at
$1-1/(b+1)^2+1/n^2$.
\end{proof}

\section{Application: adjudicating the bit-length-56 record}

The recorded quantities are pooled $\rho(T,\text{rate})=0.669$; CI $[0.650,0.690]$; validation
band $[0.55,0.85]$; pre-stated advantage bar $+0.05$; observed pooled advantage $+0.045$;
shortfall $0.005$; baseline pooled reading $0.624$.

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \emph{The primary hypothesis is comfortably inside the band}: $0.55\le0.650$ and
$0.690\le0.85$.
\item[(b)] \emph{Both statistics read far below their own ceilings}: $0.669^2=0.4476<6/7=0.8571$,
and likewise for the baseline. The shortfall is not a granularity artefact.
\item[(c)] \emph{The reweighting budget exceeds the shortfall sevenfold}: on the $\rho$ scale the
maximal gain from any stratified reweighting is
$\sqrt{\kappa^\star}-\sqrt{6/7}=0.9616465-0.9258201\in(0.0358,0.0359)>7\times0.005$.
\item[(d)] \emph{Headroom under the optimal weighting is enormous}: against
$\sqrt{\kappa^\star}=0.96165$ the recorded $0.669$ leaves $0.2926$ of unused range; against the
universal cap, $0.3308$.
\end{enumerate}

The failure of the advantage hypothesis is therefore a fact about the response variable, not a
geometric ceiling imposed by ties. Count parity in this batch is not evidence that the
trailing-zero statistic is saturated.

\section{Algorithms}

\textbf{Algorithm A (Exact ceiling).} Given $L$, compute $n=\sum m_j$ and $C=\sum m_j^3$ in
exact rational arithmetic and return $1-(C-n)/(n^3-n)$. Cost $O(K)$ big-integer operations.
Exact arithmetic matters: at $b=56$ the quantities span $10^{50}$, and double precision
destroys the $1/n^2$ corrections the sandwich is about.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Algorithm B (Cap comparison).} Return
$(1-C/n^3,\ \rmax(L),\ 1-C/n^3+1/n^2)$ and assert the sandwich, then return $1-1/K^2+1/n^2$ and
assert the block-count cap: an executable witness for Theorems~\ref{thm:sandwich}
and~\ref{thm:cap}. Cost $O(K)$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Algorithm C (Optimal stratified ratio).} Maximise
$\kappa(1,s)=1-(1+s^3/7)/(1+s)^3$ over $s>0$ by ternary search on the unimodal objective,
converging to $s^\star=\sqrt7$; alternatively enumerate the convergents of
$\sqrt7=[2;\overline{1,1,1,4}]$, namely $2,3,5/2,8/3,37/14,\dots$, reporting the first within a
target tolerance. Cost $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What the cap does and does not say}
The cap bounds \emph{achievable} correlation under the most favourable response; it says nothing
about the actual correlation of a dataset. Its value is diagnostic: when a measurement falls
short of a target, the cap says whether the instrument could possibly have reached it. The cap
is also tight only at the flat profile; for strongly unequal profiles the true ceiling is much
lower, and the exact formula~\eqref{eq:law} with a closed-form $C$ (as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:dyadic}) should be used.

\subsection{Class count, or entropy?}
Writing $f_j=m_j/n$, we have $C(L)/n^3=\sum_j f_j^3$, the probability that three independent
draws land in the same class --- a R\'enyi-type collision quantity of order $3$. The continuum
ceiling is exactly $1-\|f\|_3^3$, and the block-count cap is the standard power-mean bound
$\|f\|_3^3\ge K^{-2}$ on the simplex. Rank-correlation ceilings are thus governed by the
order-3 collision quantity of the tie distribution, and the class count is the crudest invariant
controlling it.

\subsection{The two roles of the cubic identity}
Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic} yields, with $s=\sqrt{\kappa_g}$ real, the sharp constant
$1-1/(1+\sqrt{\kappa_g})^2$ with an irrational equality case; and with $s=K$ an integer and
induction over the list, the universal power-mean bound $n^3\le K^2C(L)$. The same square
$(v-su)^2$ encodes ``the tail is $s$ times the head'': in the first case the optimal weight
ratio, in the second the flatness condition.

\subsection{Design guidance}
(1) Count classes first: $K$ bounds the ceiling at $1-1/K^2$ before any data is collected.
(2) Weighting buys a bounded, computable amount --- for binary about $0.036$ on the $\rho$
scale. (3) The best weighting is inverse-frequency, but flattening a $57$-class dyadic cascade
means upweighting a singleton by $2^{55}$, which wrecks estimator variance; the sharp stratified
cap is the realistic target. (4) Report ceilings alongside readings.

\section{Future directions}

\textbf{1. Continuum-sandwich rigidity.} The width $1/n^2$ is an upper bound on the discrete
correction; one expects it to be its exact leading order whenever the largest block is a
constant fraction of $n$. A two-sided expansion
$\rmax=1-\|f\|_3^3+c(f)/n^2+O(n^{-3})$ with $c(f)$ identified would upgrade every cap here to an
equality up to $O(n^{-3})$ and decide whether the flat profile is the exact finite-$n$
maximiser.

\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{2. Multi-statistic Gram geometry.} For $k$ statistics against one response the relevant
object is the Gram matrix of midrank vectors, and the achievable multiple correlation depends on
the joint tie structure. A block-count cap in terms of the number of cells of the common
refinement would bound what any ensemble of coarse probes can achieve.

\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{3. Sharp constants for constrained weightings.} Between two-level and fully arbitrary
lies the hierarchy of $r$-level weightings. Theorem~\ref{thm:sqrt7} handles $r=2$ and
Theorem~\ref{thm:cap} handles $r=K$; determining $\kappa^\star_r$ would interpolate, with
equality cases arising from an $r$-variable analogue of Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic}.

\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{4. Variance-aware optimality.} Maximise the ceiling subject to a bound on
$\max_j w_j/\min_j w_j$, or on the effective sample size
$(\sum w_jm_j)^2/\sum w_j^2m_j$, to obtain the weighting a practitioner should actually use.

\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{5. Radix and valuation generalisations.} The law $\kappa_g=(g^3-1)/(g-1)^3$ invites a
general theory for valuations on arbitrary discrete valuation rings and for non-geometric decay:
which decay rates $m_j\sim n\alpha^j$ admit closed-form ceilings, and what replaces
$\sqrt{\kappa_g}$ for sub-geometric cascades?

\section{Conclusion}

The ceiling on rank correlation imposed by ties is governed, uniformly over all tie profiles and
to within an additive $1/n^2$, by the number of tie classes alone: $\rmax\le1-1/K^2+1/n^2$,
sharp at the flat profile. Since reweighting redistributes mass among classes without creating
new ones, this caps every weighting scheme simultaneously. For the 2-adic zero-fit dial the
unweighted ceiling is $\sqrt{6/7}=0.92582$, the sharp two-level ceiling is
$\sqrt{1-1/(1+\sqrt7)^2}=0.96165$ attained only at $q=\sqrt7p$, and the universal ceiling at
bit-length $56$ is $0.99985$ --- all finite-length statements, thanks to the continuum sandwich.
Applied to the recorded replication, these bounds show the $0.005$ shortfall cannot be
attributed to tie geometry: the reweighting budget is seven times the shortfall and the reading
leaves $\approx0.29$ of headroom. The negative verdict is about the response variable; the
instrument is exonerated.

--------

2.  The continuum sandwich   1 - C/n^3  <=  rho^2  <=  1 - C/n^3 + 1/n^2.
3.  The power-mean bound     n^3 <= K^2 * C,     equality iff flat.
4.  The block-count cap      rho^2 <= 1 - 1/K^2 + 1/n^2,  and its sharpness.
5.  The 2-adic zero-fit dial: closed-form cubic moment (8^b + 6)/7.
6.  Stratified weightings, the sqrt(7) optimum, and the radix law.
7.  Arbitrary weightings of the bit-length-56 dial.

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from math import isqrt, sqrt
from typing import Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Profile = Sequence[int]

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Tie profiles and the exact ceiling
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def mass(profile: Profile) -> int:
    """Total number of observations n = sum_j m_j."""
    return sum(profile)


def cube_sum(profile: Profile) -> int:
    """The cubic moment C(L) = sum_j m_j^3."""
    return sum(m**3 for m in profile)


def tie_correction(profile: Profile) -> Fraction:
    """Kendall tie correction  (1/12) * sum_j (m_j^3 - m_j) = (C - n)/12."""
    return Fraction(cube_sum(profile) - mass(profile), 12)


def spearman_sq_max(profile: Profile) -> Fraction:
    """
    Exact tie-attenuation ceiling

        rho^2_max(L) = 1 - (C(L) - n) / (n^3 - n),

    the largest squared Spearman rank correlation a statistic with tie profile
    ``profile`` can achieve against any response.  Requires n >= 2.
    """
    n = mass(profile)
    if n < 2:
        raise ValueError("the ceiling requires a mass of at least 2")
    return 1 - Fraction(cube_sum(profile) - n, n**3 - n)


def continuum_ceiling(profile: Profile) -> Fraction:
    """The scale-invariant surrogate  1 - C(L)/n^3 = 1 - sum_j f_j^3."""
    n = mass(profile)
    return 1 - Fraction(cube_sum(profile), n**3)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2-4.  The three structural bounds
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def sandwich(profile: Profile) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction, Fraction]:
    """Return (lower, exact, upper) for the continuum sandwich."""
    n = mass(profile)
    lo = continuum_ceiling(profile)
    return lo, spearman_sq_max(profile), lo + Fraction(1, n**2)


def power_mean_slack(profile: Profile) -> int:
    """K^2 * C(L) - n^3, which Theorem 4.2 asserts is >= 0 (= 0 iff flat)."""
    return len(profile) ** 2 * cube_sum(profile) - mass(profile) ** 3


def block_count_cap(profile: Profile) -> Fraction:
    """The universal cap  1 - 1/K^2 + 1/n^2  depending only on K and n."""
    k, n = len(profile), mass(profile)
    return 1 - Fraction(1, k**2) + Fraction(1, n**2)


def flat_profile(k: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    """The extremiser of the block-count cap: K blocks of equal size m."""
    return [m] * k


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  The 2-adic zero-fit dial
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def dyadic_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """
    Tie profile of T(x) = nu_2(x) (trailing-zero count) on uniform b-bit draws:

        D_0 = [1],   D_{b+1} = [2^b] ++ D_b,

    i.e. D_b = [2^(b-1), 2^(b-2), ..., 2, 1, 1]:  b+1 classes, mass 2^b.
    """
    if b == 0:
        return [1]
    return [2 ** (b - 1 - k) for k in range(b)] + [1]


def dyadic_cube_sum_closed_form(b: int) -> Fraction:
    """Proposition 5.1:  C(D_b) = (8^b + 6)/7."""
    return Fraction(8**b + 6, 7)


def weight(profile: Profile, weights: Sequence[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Coordinatewise reweighting W (*) L.  Length -- the class count -- is fixed."""
    return [w * m for w, m in zip(weights, profile)]


def stratified_weights(b: int, p: int, q: int) -> List[int]:
    """Two-level weighting: p on the dominant odd class, q on every deeper class."""
    return [p] + [q] * b


def equalising_weights(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """Inverse-frequency weights 2^k flattening D_b to b+1 blocks of size 2^(b-1)."""
    return [2**k for k in range(b)] + [2 ** (b - 1)] if b >= 1 else [1]


def strat_ceiling(p: float, q: float, kappa: float = 7.0) -> float:
    """Asymptotic stratified ceiling  1 - (p^3 + q^3/kappa)/(p+q)^3."""
    return 1.0 - (p**3 + q**3 / kappa) / (p + q) ** 3


def kappa_radix(g: float) -> float:
    """Radix constant  kappa_g = (g^3 - 1)/(g - 1)^3;  kappa_2 = 7."""
    return (g**3 - 1.0) / (g - 1.0) ** 3


def strat_optimum(kappa: float) -> float:
    """Sharp maximum of the stratified ceiling:  1 - 1/(1 + sqrt(kappa))^2."""
    return 1.0 - 1.0 / (1.0 + sqrt(kappa)) ** 2


def weight_gain(kappa: float) -> float:
    """Squared-ceiling gain bought by optimal stratified weighting: 1/k - 1/(1+sqrt k)^2."""
    return 1.0 / kappa - 1.0 / (1.0 + sqrt(kappa)) ** 2


def sqrt7_convergents(count: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """Continued-fraction convergents of sqrt(7) = [2; 1,1,1,4, 1,1,1,4, ...]."""
    terms: List[int] = [2]
    cycle = [1, 1, 1, 4]
    while len(terms) < count:
        terms.append(cycle[(len(terms) - 1) % 4])
    out: List[Fraction] = []
    for i in range(1, count + 1):
        value = Fraction(terms[i - 1])
        for t in reversed(terms[: i - 1]):
            value = t + 1 / value
        out.append(value)
    return out

# helpers
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def show(label: str, value: Fraction | float, digits: int = 10) -> None:
    v = float(value)
    print(f"    {label:<52s} {v:.{digits}f}")


def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)


def rho(x: Fraction | float) -> float:

def demo_basic_ceilings() -> None:
    rule("1.  The tie-attenuation law on small profiles")
    examples: List[Tuple[str, List[int]]] = [
        ("no ties, n = 6", [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]),
        ("one constant class, n = 6", [6]),
        ("two equal classes, n = 6", [3, 3]),
        ("three equal classes, n = 6", [2, 2, 2]),
        ("lopsided 4+1+1", [4, 1, 1]),
        ("dyadic dial, b = 3", dyadic_profile(3)),
    ]
    print(f"    {'profile':<28s} {'K':>3s} {'n':>4s} {'rho^2_max':>12s} {'rho_max':>10s}")
    for name, prof in examples:
        s = spearman_sq_max(prof)
        print(

        )
    print("\n    A tie-free profile reaches 1; a single class reaches 0.")

    rule("2.  The continuum sandwich:  1 - C/n^3  <=  rho^2  <=  1 - C/n^3 + 1/n^2")

        dyadic_profile(6),

    print(f"    {'profile (K, n)':<24s} {'lower':>14s} {'exact':>14s} {'upper':>14s} {'width':>12s}")
    for prof in profiles:

        assert lo <= ex <= hi, "continuum sandwich violated"
        tag = f"K={len(prof)}, n={mass(prof)}"

    b = 56
    n = 2**b

    print(f"    (n = 2^56 = {n})")

    rule("3-4.  Power-mean bound  n^3 <= K^2 C,  and the block-count cap")
    print("    Slack K^2*C - n^3 (zero exactly on flat profiles):\n")
    tests: List[List[int]] = [
        flat_profile(4, 5),
        [5, 5, 5, 6],
        [1, 1, 1, 17],
        dyadic_profile(5),
    ]
    for prof in tests:
        slack = power_mean_slack(prof)
        flat = len(set(prof)) == 1
        print(f"      {str(prof):<34s} slack = {slack:>18d}   {'FLAT' if flat else ''}")
        assert slack >= 0, "power-mean bound violated"

    print("\n    Block-count cap versus the true ceiling:\n")
    print(f"    {'profile':<30s} {'rho^2_max':>12s} {'1-1/K^2+1/n^2':>16s}")
    for prof in tests + [dyadic_profile(10)]:
        s = spearman_sq_max(prof)
        cap = block_count_cap(prof)
        assert s <= cap, "block-count cap violated"
        print(f"    {str(prof)[:29]:<30s} {float(s):>12.8f} {float(cap):>16.8f}")

    print("\n    Sharpness: the flat profile attains 1 - 1/K^2 to within 1/n^2.\n")
    print(f"    {'K':>4s} {'m':>4s} {'1 - 1/K^2':>14s} {'rho^2_max(flat)':>18s} {'cap':>16s}")
    for k, m in [(2, 3), (5, 4), (10, 10), (57, 2**55)]:

        cap = block_count_cap(prof)
        assert lower <= s <= cap, "sharpness sandwich violated"
        print(

            f"{float(s):>18.10f} {float(cap):>16.10f}"
        )


def demo_dial() -> None:
    rule("5.  The 2-adic zero-fit dial")
    print("    Profile of T(x) = nu_2(x) on uniform b-bit draws, and its cubic moment.\n")
    print(f"    {'b':>3s} {'K = b+1':>8s} {'n = 2^b':>12s} {'C = (8^b+6)/7':>22s} {'rho_max':>11s}")

        c = cube_sum(prof)
        assert Fraction(c) == dyadic_cube_sum_closed_form(b), "closed form mismatch"

def demo_stratified_and_radix() -> None:
    rule("6.  Stratified weightings, the sqrt(7) optimum, and the radix law")
    kappa = 7.0
    opt = strat_optimum(kappa)
    print(f"    kappa* = 1 - 1/(1+sqrt 7)^2 = {opt:.10f}")
    print(f"    sqrt(kappa*)                = {sqrt(opt):.10f}")

    b = 56
    prof = dyadic_profile(b)
    k = len(prof)
    print(f"    The dial has K = b + 1 = {k} tie classes; (b+1)^2 = {k * k}.")
    print(f"    Universal cap on rho^2:  1 - 1/{k * k} + 1/n^2.\n")

    trials: List[Tuple[str, List[int]]] = [
        ("all-ones (no weighting)", [1] * k),
        ("stratified (p,q) = (1,3)", stratified_weights(b, 1, 3)),
        ("stratified (p,q) = (14,37)", stratified_weights(b, 14, 37)),

    print(f"\n    1 - 1/3249 + 2^-112  =>  rho <= {rho(universal):.10f}")

def demo_record_adjudication() -> None:
    rule("8.  Adjudicating the recorded bit-length-56 replication")
    pooled = Fraction(669, 1000)
    ci_low, ci_high = Fraction(650, 1000), Fraction(690, 1000)
    band_low, band_high = Fraction(55, 100), Fraction(85, 100)
    advantage, bar = Fraction(45, 1000), Fraction(50, 1000)
    shortfall = bar - advantage

    print("    Recorded quantities")
    show("pooled rho(T, rate)", pooled, 4)
    show("CI low / high", ci_low, 4)
    show("", ci_high, 4)
    show("validation band low / high", band_low, 4)
    show("", band_high, 4)
    show("pooled weighted advantage", advantage, 4)
    show("pre-stated bar", bar, 4)
    show("shortfall", shortfall, 4)
    show("popcount baseline reading", pooled - advantage, 4)

    assert band_low <= ci_low and ci_high <= band_high
    print("\n    (a) H1: the whole CI lies inside the validation band.  PASS")

    unweighted = spearman_sq_max(dyadic_profile(56))
    assert pooled**2 < unweighted
    print("    (b) The reading sits far below the dial's own unweighted ceiling:")
    show("rho^2 recorded", pooled**2)
    show("rho^2 ceiling (unweighted, b = 56)", unweighted)

    print("\n    (c) The reweighting budget on the rho scale:")
    show("sqrt(kappa*) - sqrt(6/7)", budget)
    show("recorded shortfall", shortfall, 4)
    show("ratio budget / shortfall", budget / float(shortfall), 4)

    print("        The budget exceeds the shortfall more than sevenfold.")

    print("\n    (d) Headroom left unused by the recorded reading:")
    show("against sqrt(kappa*) (stratified optimum)", sqrt(opt) - float(pooled))
    show("against the universal cap", sqrt(universal) - float(pooled))

    print(

        "    Tie geometry left seven times the missing margin on the table, so the\n"
        "    dial was nowhere near saturated -- count parity in this batch is not\n"
        "    evidence that the trailing-zero statistic has run out of resolution."

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from math import isqrt, sqrt
from typing import Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Profile = Sequence[int]

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Tie profiles and the exact ceiling
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def mass(profile: Profile) -> int:
    """Total number of observations n = sum_j m_j."""
    return sum(profile)


def cube_sum(profile: Profile) -> int:
    """The cubic moment C(L) = sum_j m_j^3."""
    return sum(m**3 for m in profile)


def tie_correction(profile: Profile) -> Fraction:
    """Kendall tie correction  (1/12) * sum_j (m_j^3 - m_j) = (C - n)/12."""
    return Fraction(cube_sum(profile) - mass(profile), 12)


def spearman_sq_max(profile: Profile) -> Fraction:
    """
    Exact tie-attenuation ceiling

        rho^2_max(L) = 1 - (C(L) - n) / (n^3 - n),

    the largest squared Spearman rank correlation a statistic with tie profile
    ``profile`` can achieve against any response.  Requires n >= 2.
    """
    n = mass(profile)
    if n < 2:
        raise ValueError("the ceiling requires a mass of at least 2")
    return 1 - Fraction(cube_sum(profile) - n, n**3 - n)


def continuum_ceiling(profile: Profile) -> Fraction:
    """The scale-invariant surrogate  1 - C(L)/n^3 = 1 - sum_j f_j^3."""
    n = mass(profile)
    return 1 - Fraction(cube_sum(profile), n**3)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2-4.  The three structural bounds
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def sandwich(profile: Profile) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction, Fraction]:
    """Return (lower, exact, upper) for the continuum sandwich."""
    n = mass(profile)
    lo = continuum_ceiling(profile)
    return lo, spearman_sq_max(profile), lo + Fraction(1, n**2)


def power_mean_slack(profile: Profile) -> int:
    """K^2 * C(L) - n^3, which Theorem 4.2 asserts is >= 0 (= 0 iff flat)."""
    return len(profile) ** 2 * cube_sum(profile) - mass(profile) ** 3


def block_count_cap(profile: Profile) -> Fraction:
    """The universal cap  1 - 1/K^2 + 1/n^2  depending only on K and n."""
    k, n = len(profile), mass(profile)
    return 1 - Fraction(1, k**2) + Fraction(1, n**2)


def flat_profile(k: int, m: int) -> List[int]:
    """The extremiser of the block-count cap: K blocks of equal size m."""
    return [m] * k


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  The 2-adic zero-fit dial
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def dyadic_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """
    Tie profile of T(x) = nu_2(x) (trailing-zero count) on uniform b-bit draws:

        D_0 = [1],   D_{b+1} = [2^b] ++ D_b,

    i.e. D_b = [2^(b-1), 2^(b-2), ..., 2, 1, 1]:  b+1 classes, mass 2^b.
    """
    if b == 0:
        return [1]
    return [2 ** (b - 1 - k) for k in range(b)] + [1]


def dyadic_cube_sum_closed_form(b: int) -> Fraction:
    """Proposition 5.1:  C(D_b) = (8^b + 6)/7."""
    return Fraction(8**b + 6, 7)


def weight(profile: Profile, weights: Sequence[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Coordinatewise reweighting W (*) L.  Length -- the class count -- is fixed."""
    return [w * m for w, m in zip(weights, profile)]


def stratified_weights(b: int, p: int, q: int) -> List[int]:
    """Two-level weighting: p on the dominant odd class, q on every deeper class."""
    return [p] + [q] * b


def equalising_weights(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """Inverse-frequency weights 2^k flattening D_b to b+1 blocks of size 2^(b-1)."""
    return [2**k for k in range(b)] + [2 ** (b - 1)] if b >= 1 else [1]


def strat_ceiling(p: float, q: float, kappa: float = 7.0) -> float:
    """Asymptotic stratified ceiling  1 - (p^3 + q^3/kappa)/(p+q)^3."""
    return 1.0 - (p**3 + q**3 / kappa) / (p + q) ** 3


def kappa_radix(g: float) -> float:
    """Radix constant  kappa_g = (g^3 - 1)/(g - 1)^3;  kappa_2 = 7."""
    return (g**3 - 1.0) / (g - 1.0) ** 3


def strat_optimum(kappa: float) -> float:
    """Sharp maximum of the stratified ceiling:  1 - 1/(1 + sqrt(kappa))^2."""
    return 1.0 - 1.0 / (1.0 + sqrt(kappa)) ** 2


def weight_gain(kappa: float) -> float:
    """Squared-ceiling gain bought by optimal stratified weighting: 1/k - 1/(1+sqrt k)^2."""
    return 1.0 / kappa - 1.0 / (1.0 + sqrt(kappa)) ** 2


def sqrt7_convergents(count: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """Continued-fraction convergents of sqrt(7) = [2; 1,1,1,4, 1,1,1,4, ...]."""
    terms: List[int] = [2]
    cycle = [1, 1, 1, 4]
    while len(terms) < count:
        terms.append(cycle[(len(terms) - 1) % 4])
    out: List[Fraction] = []
    for i in range(1, count + 1):
        value = Fraction(terms[i - 1])
        for t in reversed(terms[: i - 1]):
            value = t + 1 / value
        out.append(value)
    return out


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# helpers
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def show(label: str, value: Fraction | float, digits: int = 10) -> None:
    v = float(value)
    print(f"    {label:<52s} {v:.{digits}f}")


def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)


def rho(x: Fraction | float) -> float:
    return sqrt(float(x))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# demonstrations

def demo_basic_ceilings() -> None:
    rule("1.  The tie-attenuation law on small profiles")
    examples: List[Tuple[str, List[int]]] = [
        ("no ties, n = 6", [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]),
        ("one constant class, n = 6", [6]),
        ("two equal classes, n = 6", [3, 3]),
        ("three equal classes, n = 6", [2, 2, 2]),
        ("lopsided 4+1+1", [4, 1, 1]),
        ("dyadic dial, b = 3", dyadic_profile(3)),
    ]
    print(f"    {'profile':<28s} {'K':>3s} {'n':>4s} {'rho^2_max':>12s} {'rho_max':>10s}")
    for name, prof in examples:
        s = spearman_sq_max(prof)
        print(
            f"    {str(prof):<28s} {len(prof):>3d} {mass(prof):>4d} "
            f"{float(s):>12.6f} {rho(s):>10.6f}   ({name})"
        )
    print("\n    A tie-free profile reaches 1; a single class reaches 0.")


def demo_sandwich() -> None:
    rule("2.  The continuum sandwich:  1 - C/n^3  <=  rho^2  <=  1 - C/n^3 + 1/n^2")
    profiles: List[List[int]] = [
        [3, 3],
        [4, 1, 1],
        flat_profile(5, 7),
        dyadic_profile(6),
        dyadic_profile(12),
    ]
    print(f"    {'profile (K, n)':<24s} {'lower':>14s} {'exact':>14s} {'upper':>14s} {'width':>12s}")
    for prof in profiles:
        lo, ex, hi = sandwich(prof)
        assert lo <= ex <= hi, "continuum sandwich violated"
        tag = f"K={len(prof)}, n={mass(prof)}"
        print(
            f"    {tag:<24s} {float(lo):>14.10f} {float(ex):>14.10f} "
            f"{float(hi):>14.10f} {float(hi - lo):>12.3e}"
        )
    print("\n    The width is exactly 1/n^2, uniformly over all profiles.")

    b = 56
    n = 2**b
    print(f"\n    At the recorded bit-length b = {b}:  1/n^2 = 2^-112 = {2.0**-112:.4e}")
    print(f"    (n = 2^56 = {n})")


def demo_power_mean_and_cap() -> None:
    rule("3-4.  Power-mean bound  n^3 <= K^2 C,  and the block-count cap")
    print("    Slack K^2*C - n^3 (zero exactly on flat profiles):\n")
    tests: List[List[int]] = [
        flat_profile(4, 5),
        [5, 5, 5, 6],
        [1, 1, 1, 17],
        dyadic_profile(5),
    ]
    for prof in tests:
        slack = power_mean_slack(prof)
        flat = len(set(prof)) == 1
        print(f"      {str(prof):<34s} slack = {slack:>18d}   {'FLAT' if flat else ''}")
        assert slack >= 0, "power-mean bound violated"

    print("\n    Block-count cap versus the true ceiling:\n")
    print(f"    {'profile':<30s} {'rho^2_max':>12s} {'1-1/K^2+1/n^2':>16s}")
    for prof in tests + [dyadic_profile(10)]:
        s = spearman_sq_max(prof)
        cap = block_count_cap(prof)
        assert s <= cap, "block-count cap violated"
        print(f"    {str(prof)[:29]:<30s} {float(s):>12.8f} {float(cap):>16.8f}")

    print("\n    Sharpness: the flat profile attains 1 - 1/K^2 to within 1/n^2.\n")
    print(f"    {'K':>4s} {'m':>4s} {'1 - 1/K^2':>14s} {'rho^2_max(flat)':>18s} {'cap':>16s}")
    for k, m in [(2, 3), (5, 4), (10, 10), (57, 2**55)]:
        prof = flat_profile(k, m)
        lower = 1 - Fraction(1, k**2)
        s = spearman_sq_max(prof)
        cap = block_count_cap(prof)
        assert lower <= s <= cap, "sharpness sandwich violated"
        print(
            f"    {k:>4d} {m if m < 10**6 else '2^55':>4} {float(lower):>14.10f} "
            f"{float(s):>18.10f} {float(cap):>16.10f}"
        )


def demo_dial() -> None:
    rule("5.  The 2-adic zero-fit dial")
    print("    Profile of T(x) = nu_2(x) on uniform b-bit draws, and its cubic moment.\n")
    print(f"    {'b':>3s} {'K = b+1':>8s} {'n = 2^b':>12s} {'C = (8^b+6)/7':>22s} {'rho_max':>11s}")
    for b in range(1, 9):
        prof = dyadic_profile(b)
        c = cube_sum(prof)
        assert Fraction(c) == dyadic_cube_sum_closed_form(b), "closed form mismatch"
        s = spearman_sq_max(prof)
        print(f"    {b:>3d} {len(prof):>8d} {mass(prof):>12d} {c:>22d} {rho(s):>11.7f}")

    print(f"\n    Limit of the unweighted ceiling: rho -> sqrt(6/7) = {sqrt(6 / 7):.7f}")
    for b in (20, 40, 56):
        prof = dyadic_profile(b)
        print(f"      b = {b:>3d}:  rho_max = {rho(spearman_sq_max(prof)):.12f}")
    print("\n    Half the mass in one class costs a permanent 1/7 of squared resolution.")


def demo_stratified_and_radix() -> None:
    rule("6.  Stratified weightings, the sqrt(7) optimum, and the radix law")
    kappa = 7.0
    opt = strat_optimum(kappa)
    print(f"    kappa* = 1 - 1/(1+sqrt 7)^2 = {opt:.10f}")
    print(f"    sqrt(kappa*)                = {sqrt(opt):.10f}")
    print(f"    unweighted sqrt(6/7)        = {sqrt(6 / 7):.10f}")
    print(f"    reweighting budget on rho   = {sqrt(opt) - sqrt(6 / 7):.10f}")
    print("\n    Ceiling kappa(1, s) as the weight ratio s = q/p sweeps past sqrt 7:\n")
    print(f"    {'s':>10s} {'kappa(1,s)':>16s} {'kappa* - kappa':>18s}")
    for s in [1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, sqrt(7.0), 3.0, 4.0, 8.0]:
        k = strat_ceiling(1.0, s, kappa)
        marker = "   <-- optimum at s = sqrt 7" if abs(s - sqrt(7.0)) < 1e-12 else ""
        print(f"    {s:>10.6f} {k:>16.10f} {opt - k:>18.3e}{marker}")

    print("\n    Rational weightings are never optimal; convergents of sqrt 7 close in fast:\n")
    print(f"    {'q/p':>10s} {'kappa(p,q)':>16s} {'deficit':>14s}")
    for conv in sqrt7_convergents(7)[1:]:
        k = strat_ceiling(1.0, float(conv), kappa)
        print(f"    {str(conv):>10s} {k:>16.10f} {opt - k:>14.3e}")

    print("\n    Radix law  kappa_g = (g^3-1)/(g-1)^3  and the gain it permits:\n")
    print(f"    {'g':>4s} {'kappa_g':>12s} {'1 - 1/kappa_g':>16s} {'optimum':>12s} {'gain':>12s}")
    for g in (2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 10.0, 16.0):
        kg = kappa_radix(g)
        print(
            f"    {g:>4.0f} {kg:>12.6f} {1 - 1 / kg:>16.8f} "
            f"{strat_optimum(kg):>12.8f} {weight_gain(kg):>12.8f}"
        )
    print("\n    The gain is strictly positive and strictly decreasing in kappa.")


def demo_arbitrary_weightings() -> None:
    rule("7.  Arbitrary weightings of the bit-length-56 dial")
    b = 56
    prof = dyadic_profile(b)
    k = len(prof)
    print(f"    The dial has K = b + 1 = {k} tie classes; (b+1)^2 = {k * k}.")
    print(f"    Universal cap on rho^2:  1 - 1/{k * k} + 1/n^2.\n")

    trials: List[Tuple[str, List[int]]] = [
        ("all-ones (no weighting)", [1] * k),
        ("stratified (p,q) = (1,3)", stratified_weights(b, 1, 3)),
        ("stratified (p,q) = (14,37)", stratified_weights(b, 14, 37)),
        ("equalising w_k = 2^k", equalising_weights(b)),
    ]
    print(f"    {'weighting':<28s} {'K':>4s} {'rho_max':>14s} {'cap on rho':>14s}")
    for name, w in trials:
        wl = weight(prof, w)
        s = spearman_sq_max(wl)
        cap = 1 - Fraction(1, k**2) + Fraction(1, mass(wl) ** 2)
        assert len(wl) == k, "weighting changed the class count (impossible)"
        assert s <= cap, "universal cap violated"
        print(f"    {name:<28s} {len(wl):>4d} {rho(s):>14.10f} {rho(cap):>14.10f}")

    universal = 1 - Fraction(1, 3249) + Fraction(1, mass(prof) ** 2)
    print(f"\n    1 - 1/3249 + 2^-112  =>  rho <= {rho(universal):.10f}")
    print("    Attained (to within 1/n^2) by the inverse-frequency weighting w_k = 2^k.")
    print("    Note every weighting leaves K = 57: weighting never creates a tie class.")


def demo_record_adjudication() -> None:
    rule("8.  Adjudicating the recorded bit-length-56 replication")
    pooled = Fraction(669, 1000)
    ci_low, ci_high = Fraction(650, 1000), Fraction(690, 1000)
    band_low, band_high = Fraction(55, 100), Fraction(85, 100)
    advantage, bar = Fraction(45, 1000), Fraction(50, 1000)
    shortfall = bar - advantage

    print("    Recorded quantities")
    show("pooled rho(T, rate)", pooled, 4)
    show("CI low / high", ci_low, 4)
    show("", ci_high, 4)
    show("validation band low / high", band_low, 4)
    show("", band_high, 4)
    show("pooled weighted advantage", advantage, 4)
    show("pre-stated bar", bar, 4)
    show("shortfall", shortfall, 4)
    show("popcount baseline reading", pooled - advantage, 4)

    assert band_low <= ci_low and ci_high <= band_high
    print("\n    (a) H1: the whole CI lies inside the validation band.  PASS")

    unweighted = spearman_sq_max(dyadic_profile(56))
    assert pooled**2 < unweighted
    print("    (b) The reading sits far below the dial's own unweighted ceiling:")
    show("rho^2 recorded", pooled**2)
    show("rho^2 ceiling (unweighted, b = 56)", unweighted)

    opt = strat_optimum(7.0)
    budget = sqrt(opt) - sqrt(6 / 7)
    print("\n    (c) The reweighting budget on the rho scale:")
    show("sqrt(kappa*) - sqrt(6/7)", budget)
    show("recorded shortfall", shortfall, 4)
    show("ratio budget / shortfall", budget / float(shortfall), 4)
    assert budget > 7 * float(shortfall)
    print("        The budget exceeds the shortfall more than sevenfold.")

    universal = float(1 - Fraction(1, 3249) + Fraction(1, mass(dyadic_profile(56)) ** 2))
    print("\n    (d) Headroom left unused by the recorded reading:")
    show("against sqrt(kappa*) (stratified optimum)", sqrt(opt) - float(pooled))
    show("against the universal cap", sqrt(universal) - float(pooled))

    print(
        "\n    Conclusion: the shortfall is a fact about the response variable.\n"
        "    Tie geometry left seven times the missing margin on the table, so the\n"
        "    dial was nowhere near saturated -- count parity in this batch is not\n"
        "    evidence that the trailing-zero statistic has run out of resolution."
    )


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__.strip().splitlines()[0])
    demo_basic_ceilings()
    demo_sandwich()
    demo_power_mean_and_cap()
    demo_dial()
    demo_stratified_and_radix()
    demo_arbitrary_weightings()
    demo_record_adjudication()
    print("\nAll assertions passed.\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Iterator, List, Tuple


def partitions(n: int, k: int, floor: int = 1) -> Iterator[List[int]]:
    """All non-increasing lists of exactly k positive parts summing to n."""
    if k == 1:
        if n >= floor:
            yield [n]
        return
    top = n - floor * (k - 1)
    for head in range(min(top, n), floor - 1, -1):
        for rest in partitions(n - head, k - 1, floor):
            if rest[0] <= head:
                yield [head] + rest


def spearman_sq_max(profile: List[int]) -> Fraction:
    n = sum(profile)
    c = sum(m**3 for m in profile)
    return 1 - Fraction(c - n, n**3 - n)


def analyse(k: int, n: int) -> Tuple[List[int], Fraction, Fraction, Fraction]:
    best_profile: List[int] = []
    best_value = Fraction(-1)
    for p in partitions(n, k):
        v = spearman_sq_max(p)
        if v > best_value:
            best_value, best_profile = v, p
    lower = 1 - Fraction(1, k**2)
    cap = lower + Fraction(1, n**2)
    return best_profile, best_value, lower, cap


def main() -> None:
    print("Exhaustive maximisation of the tie ceiling over all profiles of K blocks, mass n")
    print()
    header = (f"{'K':>3s} {'n':>4s} {'argmax profile':<26s} {'max rho^2':>13s} "

    print(header)
    print("-" * len(header))
    for k in (2, 3, 4, 5, 6):

            prof, best, lower, cap = analyse(k, n)
            used = float((best - lower) / (cap - lower))

            assert lower <= best <= cap, "block-count sandwich violated"
            assert flat, "the maximiser was not the flat profile"
            print(f"{k:>3d} {n:>4d} {str(prof):<26s} {float(best):>13.9f} "

    print()
    print("In every case the maximiser is the flat profile, the maximum lies in the")
    print("predicted window [1 - 1/K^2, 1 - 1/K^2 + 1/n^2], and it uses a definite,")
    print("K-dependent fraction of the 1/n^2 slack -- evidence that the sandwich width")
    print("is the exact leading order of the discrete correction, not merely a bound.")

    print()
    print("Non-divisible masses (no exactly flat profile exists):")
    print(f"{'K':>3s} {'n':>4s} {'argmax profile':<26s} {'max rho^2':>13s} {'cap':>13s}")
    for k, n in ((3, 13), (4, 14), (5, 17)):

        assert best <= cap
        print(f"{k:>3d} {n:>4d} {str(prof):<26s} {float(best):>13.9f} {float(cap):>13.9f}")
    print()
    print("The maximiser is as flat as the arithmetic permits: parts differ by at most 1.")

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Sequence


def exact_ceiling(profile: Sequence[int]) -> Fraction:
    """
    Return the exact maximal squared rank correlation attainable by a statistic whose
    level sets have sizes ``profile``:

        rho^2_max = 1 - (C - n) / (n^3 - n),     C = sum_j m_j^3,  n = sum_j m_j.

    All arithmetic is exact; the caller receives a Fraction.  Cost: O(K) big-integer
    multiplications, i.e. O(K * M(log n)) bit operations.
    """
    if any(m < 0 for m in profile):
        raise ValueError("block sizes must be nonnegative")
    n = sum(profile)
    if n < 2:
        raise ValueError("the ceiling requires a mass of at least 2")
    cubic_moment = sum(m**3 for m in profile)
    return 1 - Fraction(cubic_moment - n, n**3 - n)

    """The scale-invariant surrogate 1 - C/n^3 = 1 - sum_j f_j^3 (order-3 collision term)."""
    n = sum(profile)
    return 1 - Fraction(sum(m**3 for m in profile), n**3)

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Sequence


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Certificate:
    """All quantities the two structural theorems relate, for one profile."""
    classes: int
    mass: int
    cubic_moment: int
    continuum_lower: Fraction
    exact_ceiling: Fraction
    continuum_upper: Fraction
    block_count_cap: Fraction
    power_mean_slack: int
    flat: bool


def certify(profile: Sequence[int]) -> Certificate:
    """
    Compute every bound attached to ``profile`` and verify, in exact arithmetic, that

        (sandwich)     1 - C/n^3  <=  rho^2_max  <=  1 - C/n^3 + 1/n^2
        (power mean)   n^3 <= K^2 * C,  with equality iff the profile is flat
        (cap)          rho^2_max  <=  1 - 1/K^2 + 1/n^2

    Raises AssertionError if any relation fails, so the returned object is a checked
    certificate rather than an unvalidated report.  Cost: O(K) big-integer operations.
    """
    k = len(profile)
    n = sum(profile)
    if n < 2 or k == 0:
        raise ValueError("need a nonempty profile of mass at least 2")
    c = sum(m**3 for m in profile)

    lower = 1 - Fraction(c, n**3)
    exact = 1 - Fraction(c - n, n**3 - n)
    upper = lower + Fraction(1, n**2)
    cap = 1 - Fraction(1, k**2) + Fraction(1, n**2)
    slack = k**2 * c - n**3
    flat = len(set(profile)) == 1

    assert lower <= exact <= upper, "continuum sandwich violated"
    assert slack >= 0, "power-mean bound violated"
    assert (slack == 0) == flat, "power-mean equality case violated"
    assert exact <= cap, "block-count cap violated"

    return Certificate(k, n, c, lower, exact, upper, cap, slack, flat)

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from math import sqrt
from typing import List, Tuple


def kappa_radix(g: float) -> float:
    """Cascade constant kappa_g = (g^3 - 1)/(g - 1)^3; kappa_2 = 7, kappa_10 = 111/81."""
    return (g**3 - 1.0) / (g - 1.0) ** 3


def strat_ceiling(ratio: float, kappa: float) -> float:
    """Asymptotic ceiling of the two-level weighting with q/p = ratio."""
    return 1.0 - (1.0 + ratio**3 / kappa) / (1.0 + ratio) ** 3


def ternary_search_optimum(kappa: float, lo: float = 1e-6, hi: float = 1e3,
                           iters: int = 200) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """
    Maximise the unimodal map ratio |-> strat_ceiling(ratio, kappa) by ternary search.

    Returns (argmax, max).  Each iteration shrinks the bracket by the factor 2/3, so the
    cost is O(log(1/eps)) evaluations; the true argmax is sqrt(kappa) and the true maximum
    is 1 - 1/(1 + sqrt(kappa))^2, both of which the search reproduces to machine precision.
    """
    for _ in range(iters):
        a = lo + (hi - lo) / 3.0
        b = hi - (hi - lo) / 3.0
        if strat_ceiling(a, kappa) < strat_ceiling(b, kappa):
            lo = a
        else:
            hi = b
    best = 0.5 * (lo + hi)
    return best, strat_ceiling(best, kappa)


def convergents(terms: List[int]) -> List[Fraction]:
    """Convergents of a continued fraction [a0; a1, a2, ...]."""
    out: List[Fraction] = []
    for i in range(1, len(terms) + 1):
        value = Fraction(terms[i - 1])
        for t in reversed(terms[: i - 1]):
            value = t + 1 / value
        out.append(value)
    return out


def best_rational_ratio(kappa: float, tolerance: float, terms: List[int]) -> Fraction:
    """
    Smallest continued-fraction convergent of sqrt(kappa) whose two-level ceiling is within
    ``tolerance`` of the optimum.  Exists for every positive tolerance because the
    convergents converge, but never attains the optimum when sqrt(kappa) is irrational.
    """
    optimum = 1.0 - 1.0 / (1.0 + sqrt(kappa)) ** 2
    for conv in convergents(terms):
        if optimum - strat_ceiling(float(conv), kappa) <= tolerance:
            return conv
    raise ValueError("no convergent in the supplied expansion meets the tolerance")

from __future__ import annotations

import random
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def random_profile(k: int, n: int, rng: random.Random) -> List[int]:
    """A uniformly random composition of n into k positive parts."""
    cuts = sorted(rng.sample(range(1, n), k - 1))
    parts, prev = [], 0
    for c in cuts + [n]:
        parts.append(c - prev)
        prev = c
    return parts


def collision_fraction(profile: List[int]) -> float:
    n = sum(profile)
    return float(Fraction(sum(m**3 for m in profile), n**3))


def spearman_sq_max(profile: List[int]) -> float:
    n = sum(profile)
    return float(1 - Fraction(sum(m**3 for m in profile) - n, n**3 - n))


def dyadic_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    return [2 ** (b - 1 - k) for k in range(b)] + [1]


def main() -> None:
    rng = random.Random(20261140)
    n = 4096
    ks = list(range(2, 26))
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.4))

    for k in ks:
        profs = [random_profile(k, n, rng) for _ in range(60)]
        ax1.scatter([k] * len(profs), [collision_fraction(p) for p in profs],

  const cont   = 1 - cfrac;

  const width  = toNum(1n, n**2n);

           <code>b</code> grows: half the mass sits in the single class ν=0, and that

           flatness gap above is exactly 0, and the ceiling saturates the block-count cap
           1 − 1/K² to within 1/n².`;

# Ties, Ceilings, and the Number That Caps Them All

*A guided tour of what a coarse statistic can and cannot measure.*

---

## 1. The problem in one picture

Suppose your only window into a complicated system is a **coarse statistic** — a probe that
emits just a handful of distinct readings. A popcount. A bucketised timing. Or the one we
will follow throughout: the **zero-fit dial**, which reads off

$$T(x) = \nu_2(x) = \text{number of trailing zero bits of } x.$$

On uniform $56$-bit draws, $T$ has exactly $57$ possible readings — and they are wildly
lopsided. Half of all inputs are odd and collapse into the single reading $T=0$; a quarter
into $T=1$; and so on down a geometric cascade
$$2^{55},\; 2^{54},\; \dots,\; 2,\; 1,\; 1.$$

Observations sharing a reading are **tied**: no ranking procedure can order them. That is not
a nuisance — it is a hard ceiling on how much correlation the probe can ever report, even
against a perfectly cooperative response. Our whole story is about computing that ceiling
exactly, and then discovering what governs it.

Play with the laboratory below before reading on. Slide the bit-length; switch the weighting
scheme; watch the ceiling move.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>What exactly is being computed in that panel?</b></summary>

A **tie profile** is the list $L = (m_1,\dots,m_K)$ of level-set sizes of the statistic, with
mass $n = \sum_j m_j$. Its **cubic moment** is $C(L) = \sum_j m_j^3$. The classical
tie-attenuation law says the maximum squared rank correlation attainable by a statistic with
profile $L$ against *any* response is
$$\rho^2_{\max}(L) \;=\; 1 - \frac{\sum_j (m_j^3 - m_j)}{n^3 - n} \;=\; 1 - \frac{C(L) - n}{n^3 - n}.$$
Two sanity checks: no ties ($m_j \equiv 1$) gives $C = n$ and a ceiling of $1$; a constant
statistic ($K=1$) gives $C = n^3$ and a ceiling of $0$. Everything in the panel is computed in
exact arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic — at bit-length $56$ the numbers involved exceed
$10^{50}$, and IEEE doubles would silently destroy the delicate $1/n^2$ terms that the theory
is about. For background on rank correlation and midranks, see
[Spearman's rank correlation coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spearman%27s_rank_correlation_coefficient).
</details>

---

## 2. A cleaner surrogate, and why it is safe

The exact formula is awkward to optimise: those $-m_j$ and $-n$ terms are discrete debris.
The natural surrogate is the scale-invariant **continuum ceiling**
$$\widetilde\rho^{\,2}(L) = 1 - \frac{C(L)}{n^3} = 1 - \sum_j f_j^3, \qquad f_j = m_j/n,$$
which depends only on the relative class frequencies. Note that $\sum_j f_j^3$ is exactly the
probability that three independent draws land in the same class — a
[Rényi-type collision quantity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A9nyi_entropy) of order $3$.

Is it safe to work with the surrogate? Yes, and provably so.

> **Continuum Sandwich Theorem.** For every tie profile with mass $n \ge 2$,
> $$1 - \frac{C(L)}{n^3} \;\le\; \rho^2_{\max}(L) \;\le\; 1 - \frac{C(L)}{n^3} + \frac{1}{n^2}.$$

The width $1/n^2$ is uniform over *all* profiles — no assumption on the block sizes at all.
At bit-length $56$ it is $2^{-112} \approx 2\times10^{-34}$. So every bound proved in the
clean continuum world is a bound in the real discrete world, at negligible cost. This is the
step that closes the classic adversarial objection: *a limit statement is not a finite-length
statement* — unless you prove a sandwich.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof (three lines)</b></summary>

Write $A = \frac{C-n}{n^3-n}$ (so $\rho^2_{\max} = 1-A$) and $B = \frac{C}{n^3}$.

*Lower half* ($A \le B$): cross-multiplying against positive denominators, $A \le B$ is
equivalent to $n^3(C-n) \le C(n^3-n)$, i.e. $-n^4 \le -nC$, i.e. $C \le n^3$. And indeed
$C \le n^3$ always, since $(\sum m_j)^3$ expands to $\sum m_j^3$ plus nonnegative cross terms.

*Upper half*: use the exact identity $\frac{C}{n^3} - \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{C-n}{n^3}$. Since
$C \ge n$ (because $m \le m^3$ for every nonnegative integer), that numerator is nonnegative;
and shrinking the denominator from $n^3$ to $n^3 - n$ only increases the fraction, giving
$\frac{C-n}{n^3} \le \frac{C-n}{n^3-n} = A$. $\blacksquare$
</details>

---

## 3. Can you *buy* resolution by reweighting?

Here is the move a practitioner reaches for. Give each observation a multiplicity $w$, so a
class of size $m$ becomes a class of size $w\,m$. This is not cosmetic:

$$n(W\odot L) = \sum_j w_j m_j \quad\text{(linear)}, \qquad C(W \odot L) = \sum_j w_j^3 m_j^3 \quad\text{(cubic)},$$

and the ceiling is a ratio of the two. Cubic against linear: reweighting genuinely moves the
ceiling. So how far can it go?

For the simplest scheme — weight the dominant odd class by $p$, every deeper class by $q$ —
the bit-length limit of the ceiling is
$$\kappa(p,q) = 1 - \frac{p^3 + q^3/7}{(p+q)^3}.$$
Explore its shape below, and notice where the maximum sits.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

> **The $\sqrt7$ Theorem.** For all $p>0$, $q\ge0$,
> $\kappa(p,q) \le \kappa^\star = 1 - 1/(1+\sqrt7)^2 = 0.9247639\ldots$,
> with equality **if and only if** $q = \sqrt7\,p$.

The optimal weight ratio is a quadratic irrational, so *no rational weighting is exactly
optimal* — though the [continued-fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continued_fraction)
convergent $37/14$ of $\sqrt7 = [2;\overline{1,1,1,4}]$ lands within $10^{-7}$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the one identity that does everything</b></summary>

$$(1+s)^2\left(s^2u^3 + v^3\right) - s^2(u+v)^3 = (v - su)^2\Big[(1+2s)v + s(2+s)u\Big].$$

The right-hand side is a perfect square times a form that is positive for $s,u,v \ge 0$. Set
$s=\sqrt7$, $u=p$, $v=q$: the inequality $\kappa \le \kappa^\star$ pops out, and the equality
case $v = su$ is exactly $q = \sqrt7 p$. The $7$ is not magic — it is the cubic sum of a
geometric cascade of ratio $1/2$. For a general radix $g$ the constant is
$\kappa_g = (g^3-1)/(g-1)^3$, so $\kappa_2 = 7$ and $\kappa_{10} = 111/81$, and the optimum is
$1 - 1/(1+\sqrt{\kappa_g})^2$. Keep this identity in mind: in the next section it reappears
wearing a completely different hat.
</details>

**The number that matters.** On the correlation scale the entire two-level reweighting budget
for the binary dial is
$$\sqrt{\kappa^\star} - \sqrt{6/7} = 0.9616465 - 0.9258201 \in (0.0358,\ 0.0359).$$
Careful weighting can add about three and a half correlation points, and never more.

---

## 4. Removing the restriction: the block-count cap

An adversary would object: *why only two levels?* Let them tune all $57$ weights
independently. Surprisingly, this changes the analysis not at all — because of one
observation:

> **Weighting redistributes mass among tie classes. It never creates a new one.**

And the ceiling, it turns out, is governed by the class *count*.

> **Power-Mean Bound.** For every profile of $K$ blocks with mass $n$,
> $$n^3 \le K^2\,C(L),$$
> with equality **exactly** for the flat profile $m_1 = \dots = m_K$.
>
> **Block-Count Cap.** Consequently, for every profile with $n \ge 2$,
> $$\rho^2_{\max}(L) \;\le\; 1 - \frac{1}{K^2} + \frac{1}{n^2},$$
> and this is **sharp**: the flat profile has ceiling at least $1 - 1/K^2$.

The block sizes have vanished from the statement entirely.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the inductive proof — and the reappearance of the identity</b></summary>

Induct on the length of the profile. Write $L = (m) \frown L'$ with $K' = |L'|$ blocks,
tail mass $S$, tail cubic moment $C'$, inductive hypothesis $S^3 \le K'^2 C'$. The goal is
$(m+S)^3 \le (K'+1)^2(m^3 + C')$.

Apply the identity from §3 with $s = K'$, $u = m$, $v = S$:
$$K'^2 (m+S)^3 \;\le\; (1+K')^2\left(K'^2 m^3 + S^3\right) \;\le\; (1+K')^2\left(K'^2 m^3 + K'^2 C'\right),$$
and divide by $K'^2$. The slack is $(S - K'm)^2$ times a positive form, so equality forces
the head to equal the mean of the tail at every step — i.e. flatness. $\blacksquare$

The elegance: with $s$ a real weight ratio the identity gives the *sharp irrational optimum*
$\sqrt7$; with $s$ an integer block count it gives the *universal* power-mean bound. Same
square $(v-su)^2$, two completely different theorems. (This is
[Chebyshev's / the power-mean inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_mean) in
disguise, but the inductive route is the one that exposes the structure.)
</details>

Applied to the dial at bit-length $56$, which has $K = 57$ classes:

$$\rho^2_{\max} \le 1 - \frac{1}{3249} + 2^{-112}, \qquad \rho \le 0.9998461.$$

For **any** weight vector whatsoever. And the optimiser is explicit: weight the class with
$k$ trailing zeros by $2^k$, flattening the cascade — inverse-frequency weighting, optimal to
within $1/n^2$.

merely a bound.

/-- **Power-mean bound.**  For any tie profile, `n³ ≤ K²·Σⱼmⱼ³` where `K` is the number of

lemma sum_cube_le_length_sq_mul_cubeSum (L : List ℕ) :

  | nil => simp [cubeSum]
  | cons m L ih =>
      rw [List.sum_cons, List.length_cons, cubeSum_cons]
      have hm : (0 : ℚ) ≤ (m : ℚ) := Nat.cast_nonneg m
      have hS : (0 : ℚ) ≤ (L.sum : ℚ) := Nat.cast_nonneg _
      have hK : (0 : ℚ) ≤ (L.length : ℚ) := Nat.cast_nonneg _
      have hC : (0 : ℚ) ≤ cubeSum L := by
        have := sum_le_cubeSum L
        linarith
      have hcast : (((m + L.sum : ℕ)) : ℚ) = (m : ℚ) + (L.sum : ℚ) := by push_cast; ring
      have hlen : (((L.length + 1 : ℕ)) : ℚ) = (L.length : ℚ) + 1 := by push_cast; ring
      rw [hcast, hlen]
      -- the two-block cubic inequality
      rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hK with hK0 | hKpos
      · have hS0 : (L.sum : ℚ) = 0 := by
          by_contra h
          have hSpos : (0 : ℚ) < (L.sum : ℚ) := lt_of_le_of_ne hS (Ne.symm h)
          have h3 : (0 : ℚ) < (L.sum : ℚ) ^ 3 := by positivity
          rw [← hK0] at ih
          nlinarith
        rw [hS0, ← hK0]
        nlinarith

  have hnq : (0 : ℚ) < (L.sum : ℚ) := by exact_mod_cast hn

/-! ## 2. The cap -/

/-- **Block-count cap.**  A tie profile with `K` blocks and total mass `n ≥ 2` can never
push the tie-attenuation ceiling above `1 - 1/K² + 1/n²`, whatever the block sizes. -/
theorem spearmanSq_block_count_cap (L : List ℕ) (h : 2 ≤ L.sum) :

  have hL : 0 < L.length := by

    · simp at h
    · simp
  have hn : 0 < L.sum := lt_of_lt_of_le (by norm_num) h
  have hupper := spearmanSq_continuum_upper L h
  have hlow := cubeSum_div_ge_inv_length_sq L hL hn
  linarith

theorem block_count_cap_sharp (K m : ℕ) (hK : 2 ≤ K) (hm : 1 ≤ m) :

        ≤ 1 - 1 / (K : ℚ) ^ 2 + 1 / ((flatBlocks K m).sum : ℚ) ^ 2 := by

lemma sum_le_cubeSum (L : List ℕ) : (L.sum : ℚ) ≤ cubeSum L := by
  induction L with
  | nil => simp [cubeSum]
  | cons m L ih =>

/-- The cubic moment never exceeds the cube of the mass. -/
lemma cubeSum_le_sum_cube (L : List ℕ) : cubeSum L ≤ (L.sum : ℚ) ^ 3 := by

  | nil => simp [cubeSum]
  | cons m L ih =>

      have hm : (0 : ℚ) ≤ (m : ℚ) := Nat.cast_nonneg m
      have hs : (0 : ℚ) ≤ (L.sum : ℚ) := Nat.cast_nonneg _

/-- `x ≥ 2 ⇒ x³ ≥ 8`, over `ℚ`. -/
lemma rat_cube_ge {x : ℚ} (h : 2 ≤ x) : 8 ≤ x ^ 3 := by

  nlinarith [mul_nonneg (by linarith : (0 : ℝ) ≤ x - 2)

/-! ## 1. The base-`g` trailing-zero tie profile -/

/-- Tie profile of the base-`g` trailing-zero statistic on `{0, …, g^b - 1}`:
blocks of sizes `(g-1)g^{b-1}, …, (g-1)g, (g-1)`, followed by the singleton `{0}`. -/
def gBlocks (g : ℕ) : ℕ → List ℕ
  | 0 => [1]
  | b + 1 => (g - 1) * g ^ b :: gBlocks g b

/-- In base two the profile is the dyadic one. -/
theorem gBlocks_two (b : ℕ) : gBlocks 2 b = dyadicBlocks b := by
  induction b with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ k ih => rw [gBlocks, dyadicBlocks, ih]; norm_num

  induction b with
  | zero => simp [gBlocks]
  | succ k ih =>
      rw [gBlocks, List.sum_cons, ih]
      have h : (g - 1) * g ^ k + g ^ k = ((g - 1) + 1) * g ^ k := by ring
      rw [h, Nat.sub_add_cancel hg, pow_succ]
      ring

  have hg3 : (8 : ℚ) ≤ (g : ℚ) ^ 3 := rat_cube_ge hg1
  have hne : ((g : ℚ) ^ 3 - 1) ≠ 0 := by intro hc; linarith
  have hcast : (((g - 1 : ℕ)) : ℚ) = (g : ℚ) - 1 := by
    rw [Nat.cast_sub (by omega : 1 ≤ g), Nat.cast_one]
  induction b with
  | zero => norm_num [gBlocks, cubeSum]
  | succ k ih =>

        push_cast [hcast]
        ring
      rw [h]
      field_simp
      ring
